rejected.title: Human impacts on natural systems
card: A natural system is a set of linked parts, such as soil, water, air, plants and animals. A change to one part can lead to changes in the others.
Clearing land
removing trees and plants. It leaves soil bare and exposed to wind and rain, and it removes habitat for animals.
Farming and mining
farming can use up soil nutrients and add fertiliser to rivers. Mining digs up land and can release dust and waste into the air and water.
Building
roads, roofs and paving cover soil. Rain cannot soak in, so more of it runs off into drains and rivers. Burning fuels and clearing forests can also add to climate change.
rejected.remember: People's actions change one part of a natural system, and the effects can spread to other parts.

a.q: A farmer clears a hillside of trees to plant crops. Which change to the natural system is most likely?
opts: Bare soil is more exposed to wind and rain
Rain soaks into the soil more slowly than before
Animals that nest in the trees gain more habitat
The soil is covered and protected from the rain
a.why: Trees and plants cover and hold the soil. Once they are removed, the bare soil is open to wind and rain. Habitat for animals that nest in trees is lost, not gained.
a.clue: Think about what the trees were doing for the soil.

b.q: A council in Penrith covers a large paddock with roads, roofs and paving for a new suburb. What is the most likely effect on a nearby creek?
opts: More rain runs off into the creek instead of soaking in
Less rain reaches the creek because the soil absorbs it
The creek is unaffected because the paving is on land
The creek receives the same water, but it flows more slowly
b.why: Paving and roofs cover the soil, so rain cannot soak in. More of it runs off into drains and then the creek. A change on land can still affect a river, because the parts of a natural system are linked.
b.clue: Where does rain go when the soil is covered?

draft.title: Human impacts on natural systems
card: A natural system is a set of linked parts, such as soil, water, air, plants and animals. When people change one part, the change can spread to other parts.
Clearing land
removing trees destroys habitat for animals. Trees store carbon, so clearing and burning them can release carbon dioxide, a gas that adds to climate change.
Farming and mining
farming can wash fertiliser into rivers. Mining digs up land and can release waste into water and air.
Building
roads, roofs and paving cover the soil. Rain cannot soak in, so more of it runs off into drains and rivers.
draft.remember: Human activities on land can reach rivers, air and climate, because the parts of a natural system are linked.

a.q: Rain washes fertiliser from a farm in the Riverina into a nearby river. Which change is most likely?
opts: The river receives extra nutrients from the farm
The river is unaffected because the farm is on land
Nutrients in the river fall as the fertiliser dries out
Only the farm soil changes, as fertiliser stays in place
a.why: Fertiliser can wash off farmland into rivers, so the river gains nutrients. It is not unaffected, because land and rivers are linked parts of one natural system.
a.clue: Follow where the rain carries the fertiliser.

b.q: A company clears and burns a large forest in Queensland. What is the most likely effect on the climate?
opts: Carbon stored in the trees is released as carbon dioxide
More carbon dioxide is absorbed because the land is bare
Nothing changes, because forests only affect local soil
Less carbon dioxide is made as fewer trees breathe it out
b.why: Trees store carbon, and burning them releases it as carbon dioxide, which adds to climate change. Clearing does not make the land absorb more, and forests affect more than local soil.
b.clue: Think about what trees hold inside them.

a.best: The river receives extra nutrients from the farm

b.best: Carbon stored in the trees is released as carbon dioxide

proposal.title: Human impacts on natural systems
card: A natural system is a set of linked parts, such as soil, water, air, plants and animals. When clearing, farming, mining or building changes one part, the change can spread to others.
Clearing land
clearing land for farms, mines or towns removes habitat. Trees store carbon, so clearing and burning them releases carbon dioxide, a gas that adds to climate change.
Farming
fertiliser can wash off farms into rivers. The extra nutrients feed algae, and as the algae die and rot, they use up oxygen that fish need.
Building
roads, roofs and paving stop rain soaking into the soil. More water runs off quickly into drains and rivers, so they can rise faster after storms.
proposal.remember: What people do to land can spread to rivers, living things and the climate, because each part of a natural system is linked to the others.

a.q: Rain washes fertiliser from farms in the Riverina into a nearby river. Which chain of effects is most likely?
opts: Extra nutrients feed algae, which lower oxygen for fish
Extra nutrients feed the fish, so fish numbers rise
Fertiliser poisons the algae, so the water grows clearer
Nutrients settle on the riverbed, so the water is unchanged
a.why: The nutrients feed algae, and when the algae die and rot they use up the oxygen fish need. The tempting idea that nutrients feed fish directly misses the link: the algae, not the fish, take up the nutrients.
a.clue: Which living thing in the river uses the nutrients first?

b.q: A new housing estate replaces paddocks beside a creek in western Sydney. After heavy rain, what is the most likely change to the creek?
opts: It rises faster, as more rain runs off hard surfaces
It rises more slowly, as drains hold the rain back
It rises faster, as more rain soaks into the soil
It stays lower, as roofs stop rain reaching the ground
b.why: Roofs and paving stop rain soaking in, so more water runs off quickly into drains and the creek, which rises faster. The option about rain soaking into the soil has the right effect but the wrong cause: hard surfaces mean less water soaks in, not more.
b.clue: Check both the effect and the reason given for it.
